competition_series: FSAE-Australasia (FSAE-A); [uncertain] limited/no completed FS Germany (FSG) driverless entry found in sources
summary: QUT Motorsport's Autonomous subteam began developing a driverless package for their electric FSAE car around 2020, using a public ROS2 monorepo (QUTMS_Driverless, first commit 16 Apr 2021) to build perception, SLAM, planning and control from scratch. They retrofitted their 2020/2021 electric competition car (QEV-3, nicknamed 'Lando') into QEV-3D, achieving first autonomous movement in October 2021 and entering FSAE-A in December 2022 as the second competition-ready Autonomous FSAE vehicle in Australia. In 2023 they replaced their custom navigation/planning/control stack with off-the-shelf ROS2 Nav2 packages (documented in an arXiv paper, Nov 2023), yielding large accuracy and lap-time gains. QEV-3D crashed into a wall during an EBS test just before its 2024 Trackdrive run at FSAE-A due to a path-planning correction delay, causing minor damage and ending competitive use; the team retired QEV-3D as a testbed and began a next-generation AV platform, migrating the codebase to ROS2 Jazzy through 2025-2026. The repository (3,400+ commits, 2021-2026) is one of the most complete public evidence trails of any FSAE driverless program.

ramp_phases: Mule/testbench hardware bring-up on QEV-3 'Lando' (2021, ~9-10 months to first autonomous movement)
Full-vehicle QEV-3D competition entry and iteration (Dec 2022 onward)
Off-the-shelf navigation rewrite ('Nav2 replaces custom stack') (2023, ~1 year)
Compute optimization and full Trackdrive validation (2024, ~1 year, ended in crash)
Testbed/next-gen platform + ROS2 Jazzy migration (2025-2026, ongoing)
what_slipped: The team's own README frames 2024 as their 'best chance in three years' to complete a Trackdrive, implying multiple prior seasons (2022, 2023) did not achieve a full scored Trackdrive despite entering competition - i.e., the transition from 'passes tech inspection' to 'completes dynamic events' slipped by roughly 2 seasons. In 2024, an 'unpredictable delay in path computing' caused a crash during the EBS test immediately before the team's scheduled Trackdrive run, ending QEV-3D's competitive career; this was a software latency/reliability issue surfacing at the worst possible moment (during the safety-critical EBS test), not a mechanical failure. The custom-built EKF-SLAM/pure-pursuit stack built through 2021-2022 was judged in the team's own 2023 arXiv paper to have had 'substantial deviation from ground truth' and to 'lack the sophistication needed for reliable performance,' leading to a full-stack rewrite onto Nav2 rather than incremental fixes - effectively a year of rework.
platform_prerequisites: Yes - QUT reused their existing electric competition car chassis (QEV-3, campaigned 2020/2021 in the EV class) and retrofitted it into QEV-3D rather than building a dedicated DV chassis. The EV platform (QEV-3) therefore had to exist first; the retrofit-to-first-autonomous-run took roughly 6 months (repo start Apr 2021 to first autonomous movement Oct 2021), but the underlying EV car itself was a multi-year prior program (QEV series).
ebs_design: Electromechanical/pneumatic emergency brake actuator (exact actuation medium [uncertain] from public sources - README states a 'new emergency brake actuator' was added in 2023 alongside new EBS control electronics, satisfying DT.3.2). EBS is implemented as a distinct Nav2-based 'mission' from 2024 onward (ebs_test.launch.py in mission_controller package), sharing navigation/control parameters with Trackdrive but tuned separately (per Sep 2024-Jan 2026 commits). The 2024 EBS test failure (crash into a wall) was caused by a path-planning computation delay, not an EBS actuator failure - remote stop and EBS relays activated per DT.4 but too late to prevent minor contact.
ebs_development_duration: [uncertain] EBS test mission logic present by mid-2022 (commits Jul-Dec 2022: 'ebs test mission controller', 'prep for ebs test mission'); new actuator/electronics added 2023; continuous tuning through Jan 2026 - so from first EBS-mission code to a mature, competition-tested EBS spans roughly 3.5 years, though a first working test-capable version existed within ~1 year of program start
steering_actuation: Dedicated `steering_actuator` ROS2 package with a CAN-based `steering_actuator_node` relating a target steering angle to a number of actuator rotations, using an encoder for closed-loop feedback (`/vehicle/encoder_reading`). First implemented Dec 2021, refactored Oct-Nov 2022 with statusword reporting, re-tuned from telemetry Nov 2024, and moved onto the CAN translator directly Oct 2024. Per DT.2.2 the actuator must be mechanically decoupled/coupled between manual and autonomous modes; the repo includes a dedicated steering-actuator machine launch and calibration nodes (`step_response_calibration`) to characterize the stepper-motor-driven actuator. [uncertain] exact motor model, gearing ratio, and mounting location not confirmed from public sources.
brake_actuation: [uncertain] Distinct from EBS, service-brake actuation for normal autonomous driving is referenced only indirectly (accel/brake command topics `/control/accel_command`); exact actuator hardware for non-emergency braking not confirmed in public sources.
sensor_mounting_packaging: [uncertain] Not documented in detail publicly; ZED2i camera and Velodyne VLP-32C LiDAR are run through separate compute ('jetson_machine' for vision, 'roscube_machine'/LattePanda Sigma for main compute), implying at least a two-node onboard compute architecture with sensors likely distributed between a forward-facing camera/LiDAR pod and a main compute enclosure.
chassis_impact: QEV-3D is a retrofit of the existing QEV-3 EV competition chassis rather than a purpose-built DV chassis; specific structural/bodywork modifications are not detailed in public sources. [uncertain]
compute_platform: Primary/main compute: ADLINK RoScube industrial robotic controller (2022-2024) replaced by a LattePanda Sigma SBC (Intel Core i5-13490P, 13th-gen, 12-core/16-thread, up to 32GB RAM, 146x102mm, 305g) from late 2024 onward for size/weight/aero reasons, running Ubuntu/Docker/ROS2 with native x86 support for YOLOv8. Secondary compute: an NVIDIA Jetson-class 'jetson_machine' node runs the camera driver and vision pipeline detector. [uncertain] whether a separate safety MCU exists distinct from the CAN-based vehicle_supervisor node.
sensor_suite: Velodyne VLP-32C LiDAR (180-deg config per package `VLP32C.yaml`), Stereolabs ZED2i stereo camera, SBG Ellipse-D INS (IMU+GNSS, per arXiv paper), wheel-speed Hall-effect sensors, steering-angle Hall-effect sensor read over CAN via `canbus_translator_node`.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: `vehicle_supervisor_node` reads/writes CAN messages to integrate DV state with the car's shutdown circuit, publishing `/vehicle/res_status` and `/system/as_status`/`/system/shutdown`/`/system/reset` topics; RES (Remote Emergency Stop) topic/message integration added Mar 2022 (PR #115 'res-software-integration'). EBS relay and remote-stop relay behavior (DT.4.2/DT.4.3) implemented in the mission_controller's ebs_test and trackdrive handlers. [uncertain] exact relay wiring/schematic not public.
remote_stop_system: RES (Remote Emergency Stop) integrated via CAN starting Mar 2022 (`/vehicle/res_status` topic); [uncertain] specific RES hardware vendor (e.g., Bosch/AlfaOne-style unit common in FSAE-A) not confirmed from public sources.
status_indicators: [uncertain] Not explicitly documented in the reviewed sources; DSSI/ASSI/alert-sound implementation details were not found in the public repo excerpts reviewed.
custom_pcbs: [uncertain] QUT Motorsport is known to develop custom electronics for their EV program broadly (e.g., 'Electrical Control System V4' sponsored via PCBWay), but DV-specific custom PCB details and design/fab/bring-up durations were not found in the sources reviewed.
software_stack: ROS2 monorepo (QUTMS_Driverless) with Python and C++ nodes, Docker-based dev environment, Conda/RoboStack package management, pre-commit CI (GitHub Actions). Architecture: sensor drivers -> perception (vision_pipeline, lidar_pipeline) -> SLAM (custom EKF-SLAM through 2022, then Nav2's slam_toolbox from 2023) -> planning (custom planners through 2023, then Nav2 smac_planner_hybrid) -> control (custom pure pursuit through 2023, then Nav2 regulated_pure_pursuit) -> mission_controller state machine for Inspection/Trackdrive/EBS-test missions.
ros_version: ROS2, migrated Foxy (Nov 2021) -> Galactic (2022) -> Humble (Aug 2022-2024, primary distro for the Nav2 rewrite and arXiv paper) -> Jazzy (migration begun Dec 2024, merged to master by early-mid 2026).
perception_approach: Dual-modality: camera-based cone detection starting with YOLOv3/darknet (Jul 2021) then YOLOv5 (Aug-Dec 2021) via a `vision_pipeline` PyTorch/TensorRT/HSV detector on ZED2i RGB+depth; LiDAR-based cone detection via a `lidar_pipeline` using ground-plane segmentation and clustering (Total Least Squares line fitting, segment/bin classification, 2021) on Velodyne VLP-32C point clouds. Detections fused prior to SLAM. By 2024 the vision detector had migrated toward YOLOv8 (per LattePanda case study). [uncertain] exact fused perception range achieved.
slam_localization_approach: Custom EKF-SLAM (landmark-based, cone-tracking) built 2022 with variants keyed to different localization inputs (IMU, wheel-speed, SBG GPS, generic odom -> `py_slam` package's `imu_slam`/`wss_slam`/`sbg_slam`/`odom_slam` nodes, plus a C++ `node_ekf_slam`). Replaced in 2023 with ROS2 Nav2's `robot_localization` (EKF sensor fusion of GPS/IMU/wheel encoders) for state estimation plus `slam_toolbox` (laser-scan-based occupancy-grid SLAM) for mapping - a shift from a bespoke landmark-EKF to mature occupancy-grid SLAM that improved pose-tracking RMSE from 0.46+/-0.03 m to 0.06+/-0.01 m and cone-position RMSE from 1.06+/-0.05 m to 0.08+/-0.01 m in carpark testing (arXiv:2311.14276).
planning_approach: Early: reactive midpoint-following and quadratic curve-fitting controllers (2021-2022) acting almost as combined planner+controller. Mid: dedicated `planners` package (from Oct 2022) with a Delaunay-triangulation-derived and 'ordered mid spline' planner interpolating track boundaries into a driveable path (2023). Current: Nav2's `smac_planner_hybrid` A* global planner configured for Ackermann steering with curvature/boundary penalties, replacing the custom planner in 2023 - reduced lap distance ~3% (149.96m -> 145.95m) and steering-curvature demand ~5% versus the midline planner in the team's own benchmark.
control_approach: Lateral: pure pursuit, first prototyped mid-2022, ported to C++ with KDTree waypoint search in 2023 (~10x performance gain over the Python version), then replaced by Nav2's `regulated_pure_pursuit` controller in 2023-2024 (target ~8 m/s, 2.5 m lookahead), yielding an 8-9% cross-track RMSE improvement and ~0.7 s/lap gain versus the custom implementation. MPC was explored in Feb 2022 but not adopted for production. Longitudinal: a dedicated `velocity_controller` node maps target velocity/motor RPM to accel commands; EBS/Trackdrive missions share the Nav2 control stack with mission-specific parameter sets.
simulation_tooling: `eufs_sim` - a QUT-maintained hard fork of Edinburgh University Formula Student's ROS2/Gazebo driverless simulator - used from the project's earliest weeks (ROS2 fs_msgs and sim bridge built Apr 2021) for perception and control algorithm development before hardware access, and continuously thereafter for regression testing of planner/control changes.
ci_cd_testing: GitHub Actions pre-commit workflow (`.github/workflows/pre_commit.yaml`) enforcing formatting/lint (clang-format, pre-commit hooks) on every PR; no evidence of a dedicated HIL bench found in public sources, though the 'pushcart steering testing' work (Nov 2025-Jan 2026) functions as a lightweight rig for validating steering/planner behavior off the full vehicle. [uncertain] extent of automated integration/regression test suites beyond linting.
data_logging: `rosbag_creator` operations package automates rosbag recording (Popen-based service calls from EBS/Trackdrive mission handlers, reworked Oct-Nov 2024 to be triggerable via Foxglove); `rosboard` (submodule, kept updated to latest per Dec 2025 commit) provides a web-based live telemetry dashboard; `topic_to_csv` node exports arbitrary topic data to CSV for offline analysis.
open_source_repos: https://github.com/QUT-Motorsport/QUTMS_Driverless (main monorepo, 3,400+ commits since Apr 2021 - extremely useful as a ground-truth timeline and package-evolution reference); https://github.com/QUT-Motorsport/eufs_sim (simulator fork); https://github.com/QUT-Motorsport/QUTMS_Nav_Integration (Nav2 integration work referenced in the arXiv paper).
critical_path_items: 1) Getting a reliable, low-latency perception+SLAM+planning loop - the team's own analysis (arXiv 2311.14276) shows their custom stack was the accuracy bottleneck for two years, gating any move to full-speed autonomous laps. 2) EBS/safety-system maturity under real dynamic conditions - the 2024 crash during the EBS test (immediately pre-Trackdrive) shows the emergency-stop path itself was the last, and ultimately schedule-ending, validation gate each season. 3) Compute platform constraints (size/weight/thermal on the industrial RoScube) that were only resolved in late 2024 with the LattePanda Sigma swap, after 3+ seasons of competing with a heavier/bulkier compute solution.
long_lead_procurement: [uncertain] Specific lead times in weeks were not published, but inferable long-lead items typical of this stack include: Velodyne VLP-32C LiDAR, SBG Ellipse-D INS, and the industrial RoScube controller (later replaced) - all specialized/low-volume hardware items commonly cited by FSAE-DV teams as multi-month lead times; QUT's own public sources do not state numeric lead times.
first_static_test_date: [uncertain] Not explicitly dated in public sources; likely late 2021 concurrent with 'perception and control tested on Lando' (Nov 2021).
first_dynamic_test_date: October 2021 (QEV-3D 'was able to drive itself' - first remote controlled, then under its own autonomous processes, per team README).
testing_hours_before_first_comp: [uncertain] not quantified in public sources; qualitative evidence indicates months of 2021 hardware/software debugging plus an on-track data-gathering session with a safety driver in Dec 2021 ahead of the Dec 2022 competition entry.
validation_strategy: Staged mission structure mirrors competition dynamic events: `inspection.launch.py` (simple sine steering sweep for tech inspection), `ebs_test.launch.py` (reactive control + EBS relay check), `trackdrive.launch.py` (full discovery-lap mapping, planning, and 10-lap following). The team also ran controlled carpark end-to-end tests of the full Nav2 stack before competition deployment (arXiv:2311.14276) and used the same EBS-test mission logic for on-track pre-Trackdrive checks - which is also where the 2024 crash occurred, showing the validation gate itself carries residual risk if planner latency is not fully characterized.
rules_compliance_challenges: DT.3.2 EBS reliability under dynamic conditions was the hardest requirement in practice - the team passed technical inspection multiple years but the Dec 2024 EBS-test crash shows that satisfying the letter of DT.3.2 (having a compliant EBS relay/actuator chain per DT.4) did not guarantee safe real-world EBS-maneuver behavior when triggered by an errant path-planning correction. DT.2.2 actuator decoupling for steering was addressed via a dedicated steering-actuator package with manual/autonomous mode handling, iterated over several years (2021, 2022 refactor, 2024 re-tuning).
tech_inspection_experience: Passed all technical inspections at FSAE-A Dec 2022 on the team's first competition attempt, described as the '2nd competition-ready FSAE Autonomous Vehicle' in Australia - a strong first-attempt pass. [uncertain] whether any items failed on the first inspection attempt specifically (not detailed in public sources).
ebs_test_experience: Passed EBS-related checks in earlier seasons (EBS test mission logic present since mid-2022), but the Dec 2024 FSAE-A EBS test ended in a crash: a path-computation delay caused a sharp steering correction at 40 km/h just before the finish line, sending QEV-3D into a wall/tyre barrier; remote stop and EBS were both triggered but could not fully arrest the vehicle before impact, causing minor single-corner suspension damage. This ended QEV-3D's competitive career.

reliability_notes: Dec 2024 FSAE-A: off-course/crash event caused by a path-planning computation delay during the EBS test, resulting in a wall/tyre-barrier strike at 40 km/h and minor single-corner suspension damage; no structural, tractive, or electronic components affected. This was the team's most consequential DNF/incident and directly ended the QEV-3D program.
top_mistakes: 1) Spending roughly two years (2021-2022) building a fully custom EKF-SLAM + planner + pure-pursuit stack that their own later analysis showed had 'substantial deviation from ground truth' and was not competition-reliable, rather than adopting mature ROS2 Nav2 packages earlier - the 2023 rewrite alone delivered 87-93% accuracy improvements. 2) Running a heavier/bulkier industrial compute unit (ADLINK RoScube) for three-plus seasons before switching to a much smaller SBC (LattePanda Sigma) in late 2024, incurring an unnecessary aero/packaging/mass penalty for years. 3) The 2024 crash demonstrates that EBS-maneuver latency/path-computation timing had not been fully hardened even in the vehicle's final competitive season - a critical-path safety behavior that was still failing under live conditions after 4 years of development.
advice_for_new_teams: [uncertain] No direct quoted advice from QUT Motorsport to other teams was found in the sources reviewed; inferred guidance from their own documented experience: prefer mature, off-the-shelf navigation stacks (Nav2) over custom SLAM/planning/control from the start, as QUT's own paper concludes 'off-the-shelf software leads to higher-performing solutions that can be developed upon more rapidly compared to developing in-house solutions,' and custom approaches 'lack the sophistication needed for reliable performance' without substantial time and experience to mature.

QUT Motorsport overall runs at roughly 50 students across all vehicle programs (37 travelled to the 2023 national competition per public sources); package `<maintainer>` tags in the repo show a rotating cast of roughly 10-12 named individual contributors/maintainers across packages (e.g., Alastair Bradford, Alistair English, Grant van Breda, Thomas Fraser, Walden Leung, Alex Bradbury, Claudia Kiss, Calvin Johnson, Liam Ferrante), consistent with a compact, mostly-software-focused DV subteam.
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: [uncertain] Not explicitly documented; circumstantial evidence of turnover management includes consistent per-package `package.xml` maintainer fields (naming current owners), a PR template, pre-commit CI to enforce consistency across contributors, and a public monorepo/README that itself functions as onboarding documentation summarizing each season's progress for incoming members.
budget_estimate: [uncertain] No total or per-year USD/AUD budget figures were found in public sources for the DV program specifically.
recommended_sequence: Based on QUT's own trajectory and later self-critique: 1) Stand up a simulator (e.g., eufs_sim/Gazebo) and get a full sensor-to-control loop running in sim before any hardware exists. 2) Retrofit an existing EV chassis with sensors and basic drive-by-wire (steering actuator, CAN read of speed/steering) to get a moving mule as early as possible - QUT achieved this in ~6 months from repo start. 3) Adopt mature ROS2 Nav2 packages (robot_localization, slam_toolbox, smac_planner_hybrid, regulated_pure_pursuit) from the outset rather than building custom SLAM/planning/control, since QUT's own data shows this saves roughly a year of rework and produces dramatically better accuracy. 4) Build the EBS/safety mission logic in parallel with, not after, the driving stack, and stress-test the EBS maneuver specifically under realistic planner-latency conditions, since that was QUT's ultimate failure point in 2024. 5) Optimize compute platform size/weight only after the software stack is proven - QUT deferred this to year 4, which was survivable but not ideal.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: Highly applicable as a cautionary tale on sequencing: a team with a running EV and ~9 software-focused members over 24 months should skip QUT's 2021-2022 custom-SLAM detour entirely and go straight to ROS2 Nav2 building blocks (robot_localization + slam_toolbox + smac_planner_hybrid + regulated_pure_pursuit), which is exactly the architecture QUT converged on after 2+ years of learning the hard way. QUT's repo is also a strong reference for realistic package layout (perception/navigation/control/operations separation) and for how much iteration EBS-mission logic needs before it is truly safe - a 24-month team should budget explicit, repeated EBS-maneuver-under-latency testing rather than treating EBS as a checkbox, given QUT's crash occurred in year 4 of development, not year 1.
